newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-East German generals jailed for Wall killings.
newsitem.headline: Ex-East German generals jailed for Wall killings.

text.p: A Berlin court on Friday found four former East German army generals guilty of aiding manslaughter and attempted manslaughter for ordering border guards to shoot refugees trying to escape to the West.
A former East German deputy defence minister Joachim Goldbach and three other ex-generals were handed sentences ranging from over three years in prison to 22 months probation.

In sentencing the four men, aged between 67 and 70, presiding judge Ralph Ehestaedt said they bore a personal responsibility for the deaths at the Berlin Wall and the Cold War-era border between the two Germanys.
"It was not the system that behaved inhumanely but the self-declared leadership which accepted the deaths of those who thought differently or wanted to live elsewhere," Ehestaedt said in the verdict.
The defendants had disputed the existence of an order to shoot those trying to escape and insisted on their compliance with East German law and their fulfilment of duty as soldiers.
During the 21-month trial, the Berlin court heard charges against the generals who had served in the defence ministry in communist East Germany.
The court found that the four generals had approved so-called Order 101, the shoot-to-kill order for guards to fortify the Wall, as well as the laying of land mines along the former border.
The 67-year-old Goldbach and a top general in the former East German National People's Army (NVA), Harald Ludwig, also 67, each received sentences of three years and three months in prison.

Former chief inspector in the NVA, Heinz Handke, 70, was handed a two year and 10 month sentence. Fritz Peter, the 69-year-old former head of the civil defence corps, was given a 22-month suspended sentence.
The court said Peter had been the only defendant who had shown "a significant measure of regret."
Prosecutor Wolfgang Jordan, who had argued for sentences of up to four years in prison for the generals, told reprorters he was satisfied with the verdict.

The extreme secrecy surrounding East Germany's fortified borders has prevented a final count of those who were shot dead or killed by landmines as they tried to flee west from the 1950s until the the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989.
A group called the August 13 Society, named after the day the Wall was built in 1961, said its research had uncovered at least 807 deaths along the border.
Berlin courts have convicted dozens of lower-ranking border guards of manslaughter but given most of them suspended sentences because they were young recruits following orders.
The German Constitutional Court ruled last November that leaders from former East Germany could be jailed in connection with Cold War killings along the Berlin Wall and the former border.
Originally eight high-ranking East German officers were charged in the case but the court ruled that four of them were too ill to stand trial, but charges were not dropped against them.
